statement: Deep Q-learning replaces the tabular Q-learning update with a neural network Q(s,a;θ) trained by minimizing the squared error between Q(s_t,a_t;θ) and a bootstrapped target y_t, where y_t = r_t if s_{t+1} is terminal and y_t = r_t + γ max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ) otherwise (Equations 8.2–8.3, Algorithm 10).
conditions: Environment assumed to be a fully observable MDP with a finite/discrete action space; the network outputs one action value per discrete action in a single forward pass.
limits: The text states this naive extension of Q-learning 'suffers from two important issues': the moving target problem and correlation of consecutive samples (p. 215).

statement: The book defines the 'deadly triad' (citing Sutton and Barto 2018; van Hasselt et al. 2018) as the combination of off-policy learning, function approximation, and bootstrapped targets, and states this combination 'can lead to unstable and diverging value estimates.'
conditions: Applies to algorithms combining all three components simultaneously, e.g., deep Q-learning with off-policy (ε-greedy) experience.
limits: The book states divergence, as it explains the mechanism, requires all three components together: removing function approximation, bootstrapping, or off-policy sampling individually prevents the described divergence mechanism (p. 217–218).

statement: A target network with parameters θ−, initialized as a copy of the main value network and updated only periodically by copying θ, is used to compute bootstrapped targets (Equation 8.4) so that target values remain fixed between updates, reducing instability from the moving target problem (Algorithm 11).
conditions: Target network shares the main network's architecture; its parameters are copied at a set interval rather than trained by gradient descent.
limits: none

statement: The book states that RL violates both parts of the i.i.d. assumption underlying most machine learning: consecutive experience samples are correlated because s_{t+1} and r_t are determined by the transition function conditioned on s_t and a_t, and the sampling distribution shifts as the policy changes; a replay buffer D storing past transitions, from which mini-batches are sampled uniformly at random (B ~ U(D)), is introduced to break these correlations (Algorithm 12 / DQN).
conditions: The replay buffer is implemented as a fixed-capacity FIFO queue; it can only be used for off-policy algorithms because stored experiences were generated by earlier versions of the behavior policy.
limits: The text explicitly states a replay buffer 'cannot be used to update a policy following the policy gradient theorem' (p. 227) since on-policy algorithms require data generated by the current policy.

statement: In a single-agent 8x8 level-based-foraging item-collection task, an ablation compares deep Q-learning, deep Q-learning + target network, deep Q-learning + replay buffer, and full DQN (target network + replay buffer) over 100,000 time steps, five seeds; only the full DQN combination yields 'a stable and quick increase in performance and convergence to near-optimal discounted returns' (Figure 8.3), while target networks alone give 'no notable improvement' and a replay buffer alone remains 'noisy across runs.'
section: 8.1.4 Putting It All Together: Deep Q-Networks
conditions: Task: single-agent 8x8 grid item collection (no 'levels', collection always successful); hyperparameters: γ=0.99, α=3e-4, batch size 512, buffer capacity 10,000, target update every 100 steps, ε decayed 1.0→0.05 over 50,000 steps.
limits: Single fixed small-scale single-agent task; not a general claim about DQN component necessity across environments.

statement: DQN is stated to be 'prone to overestimation of action values' because the target uses max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ); double deep Q-networks (DDQN) reduces this by decoupling greedy action selection (via the main network's arg max) from action-value evaluation (via the target network), per Equation 8.6.
conditions: Requires both a main value network and a target network, as in standard DQN.
limits: none

statement: The book states that combining DDQN, prioritized experience replay (Schaul et al. 2016), parameterized exploration noise (Fortunato et al. 2018), dueling value/advantage decomposition (Wang et al. 2016), and distributional value learning (Bellemare, Dabney, and Munos 2017) yields the Rainbow algorithm, 'shown to exhibit significantly higher performance than DQN across Atari games (Hessel et al. 2018).'
conditions: Comparison reported by Hessel et al. 2018 on the Atari benchmark, cited secondhand by this textbook.
limits: The textbook does not reproduce the Rainbow experiment itself; it cites Hessel et al. 2018 for the performance claim.

statement: The policy gradient theorem's expectation is defined under the state distribution Pr(s|π) and action distribution π(·|s;ϕ) of the current policy π being optimized; the book states this 'clearly illustrates the restriction that follows from the policy gradient theorem: the optimization of the parameterized policy is limited to on-policy data' and that data from any different policy π′ — including older versions of π obtained earlier in training — 'can not be used to update π following the policy gradient theorem.'
conditions: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton and Barto 2018) as stated by the authors; applies to episodic environments; requires a differentiable policy parameterization.
limits: Q^π(s,a) in the theorem must itself be approximated since it is not known a priori; the book notes DQN-style algorithms do not satisfy the on-policy requirement because they approximate the optimal value function via the Bellman optimality equation instead.

statement: REINFORCE (Williams 1992) instantiates the policy gradient theorem with Monte Carlo estimates of episodic returns, minimizing L(ϕ) = -(1/T) Σ_t (Σ_{τ≥t} γ^{τ-t} r_τ) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equations 8.15–8.16, Algorithm 13); the book states 'Monte Carlo return estimates have high variance, which leads to high variance of gradients and unstable training in REINFORCE' because returns depend on the entire episode's states and actions.
conditions: Requires full episode rollouts (updates occur after episode termination); on-policy Monte Carlo returns.
limits: High-variance gradients are stated as an explicit limitation of the base algorithm without a baseline.

statement: The book derives (Equations 8.17–8.27) that subtracting any baseline b(s), defined only over the state s, from Q^π(s,a) in the policy gradient theorem leaves the expected gradient unchanged, because Σ_a b(s)∇_ϕπ(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ 1 = 0; a state-value function V(s;θ), trained by minimizing L(θ)=(1/T)Σ_t(u_t - V(s_t;θ))², is given as a common baseline choice.
conditions: The baseline must be a function of state only (not of the action) for the derivation to hold.
limits: none

statement: Actor-critic algorithms use a critic V to compute bootstrapped return estimates (Equations 8.30–8.32) instead of full Monte Carlo returns; the book states this gives two benefits — updates from a single time step's experience rather than waiting for episode end, and lower variance than Monte Carlo returns — 'at a price of introduced bias, because the used value function might not (yet) approximate the true expected returns of states.'
conditions: Requires a trained critic V(s;θ); the bootstrapped estimate uses one-step (or N-step) lookahead.
limits: Bias is explicitly acknowledged as the cost of bootstrapping; the book states 'we find that the trade-off of bias for lower variance often improves training stability' without a formal bound.

statement: Using a critic trained with A2C (N=5) in the single-agent level-based-foraging task, the book reports that measured variance of N-step return estimates increases with N (approaching Monte Carlo variance at N=T) while measured bias decreases with N (approaching zero, the unbiased Monte Carlo case), shown for N∈{1,...,10} plus Monte Carlo in Figure 8.5.
conditions: Measured post hoc from 10,000 evaluation episodes collected with a policy trained for 100,000 time steps with N=5 in one specific environment.
limits: Single environment, single trained policy; the book presents this to illustrate the general bias-variance trade-off qualitatively, not as a quantitative law for other tasks.

statement: Advantage actor-critic (A2C) estimates the advantage Adv(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s), approximated using the critic as Adv(s_t,a_t) = r_t - V(s_t;θ) if s_{t+1} terminal else r_t + γV(s_{t+1};θ) - V(s_t;θ) (Equation 8.36), and minimizes the actor loss L(ϕ) = -Adv(s_t,a_t) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equation 8.38) jointly with a critic squared-error loss (Equation 8.40); the book denotes its presented pseudocode 'Simplified A2C' since the original A2C/A3C (Mnih et al. 2016) also uses multi-step returns and entropy regularization.
conditions: Requires both actor π(·;ϕ) and critic V(·;θ) networks trained jointly (Algorithm 14).
limits: The book explicitly flags its Algorithm 14 as a simplification of the original A2C/A3C algorithm.

statement: Entropy regularization adds the negative policy entropy, -H(π(·|s;ϕ)) = Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) log π(a|s;ϕ) (Equation 8.41), to the actor loss; the book states that maximizing entropy 'penalizes the policy for assigning a very high probability to any action' and 'discourages premature convergence to a suboptimal close-to-deterministic policy,' thereby incentivizing exploration.
conditions: Applied as an additional term added to the actor loss; the original A2C/A3C uses it, while the book's 'Simplified A2C' (Algorithm 14) omits it by default.
limits: none

statement: PPO (Schulman et al. 2017, clipped-objective variant) computes an importance sampling ratio ρ(s,a) = π(a|s;ϕ)/π_β(a|s) (Equation 8.42) between the policy being optimized and the behavior policy that generated the data, and minimizes L(ϕ) = -min(ρ(s_t,a_t)·Adv(s_t,a_t), clip(ρ(s_t,a_t), 1-ε, 1+ε)·Adv(s_t,a_t)) (Equation 8.43, Algorithm 15); this clipping lets PPO reuse the same batch of data for N_e update epochs, unlike standard on-policy policy gradient methods that require freshly on-policy data for every update.
conditions: ε is a hyperparameter bounding how far the updated policy's action probability may diverge from π_β; requires a critic for the advantage estimate (Equation 8.36).
limits: The book describes only the clipped-surrogate PPO variant in detail, noting Schulman et al. (2017) also propose a KL-divergence-penalty variant that it does not detail.

statement: The book contrasts trust region policy optimization (TRPO, Schulman et al. 2015), which 'constrains each optimization step... to a small trust region' but 'requires either solving a constrained optimization problem or computing a penalty term, which are both computationally expensive,' with PPO's clipped surrogate objective, described as computationally efficient.
conditions: The comparison is qualitative/conceptual, not a reported head-to-head experiment in this chapter.
limits: No empirical comparison of TRPO vs. PPO is presented in this section; the comparison is descriptive.

statement: In the single-agent level-based-foraging task (Figure 8.3(a)), REINFORCE, A2C (N=5), and PPO (N=5, ε=0.2, N_e=4 epochs) are trained for 100,000 time steps across five seeds (Figure 8.6): REINFORCE 'learns to solve the task in most runs' but with 'high variance... all throughout training'; A2C and PPO with N-step returns 'reach the optimal performance across all runs within 60,000 time steps'; PPO 'is able to learn slightly faster than A2C, which can be explained by its optimization being able to use each batch of experiences multiple times.'
conditions: Small actor/critic networks (two layers, 32 hidden units), γ=0.99; REINFORCE learning rate 1e-3 without baseline; A2C/PPO learning rate 3e-4, N=5.
limits: Single fixed small-scale single-agent task; not a general ranking claim across environments.

statement: Because 'on-policy policy gradient algorithms cannot make use of a replay buffer,' the book presents synchronous data collection (parallel environment instances, agent waits for all threads each step, Algorithm 16/Figure 8.7) and asynchronous training (each thread holds its own agent copy and environment, updates a shared central network, Figure 8.9) as the two techniques used instead to break correlations and obtain larger batches for on-policy algorithms.
conditions: Both techniques assume multiple environment instances can be run in parallel; the book notes this assumption fails for single-instance physical systems such as a real robot.
limits: The book states these are 'two conceptually simple ideas' and that more complex large-scale parallelization schemes exist in the literature (citing Espeholt et al. 2018, 2020) but are not detailed here.

statement: In a 12x12 level-based-foraging task requiring collection of two items, simplified A2C is trained for five minutes with K ∈ {1,4,16,64} synchronous environments (Figure 8.8): smaller K is comparably sample-efficient per time step but less stable (K=1 'does not converge to the optimal policy'), while larger K is more wall-clock efficient, though 'these benefits diminish with a growing number of synchronous environments' due to threads idling while waiting for the slowest thread.
conditions: γ=0.99, learning rate 1e-3, N-step returns with N=10, small actor/critic networks (two 32-unit layers); wall-clock training capped at five minutes.
limits: Single environment and hardware setup; the text notes idle-time cost grows with K, so the reported trend is not claimed to hold at arbitrarily large K.

statement: For partially observable environments, the book states that value functions and policies 'should be conditioned on the episodic history of observations, h_t = (o_0,...,o_t)'; rather than concatenating or zero-padding the growing history (called impractical, and for zero-padding 'not applicable to tasks with potentially infinite episodes'), it recommends using a recurrent neural network to process the history one observation at a time, with GRUs and LSTMs cited as the RNN architectures 'commonly used in deep RL.'
section: 8.3 Observations, States, and Histories in Practice
conditions: All chapter-8 algorithms were formalized assuming full state observability (fully observable MDP, p. 213); this section states the architectural change (adding an RNN) needed to apply them under partial observability instead.
limits: The book does not re-derive the DQN/policy-gradient losses for the partially observable case in this section; it states only that the architectural substitution is what is required.

statement: Chapter 8 formalizes deep Q-learning/DQN and the policy gradient/actor-critic family (REINFORCE, A2C, PPO) entirely for single-agent RL under a fully observable MDP with discrete action spaces (stated at the chapter's outset, p. 213, and for policy representation, p. 225: 'we focus on policy gradient algorithms for discrete action spaces'); none of the empirical demonstrations in this chapter (Figures 8.3, 8.5, 8.6, 8.8) involve more than one learning agent or a continuous action space, so this chapter's results are not evidence for multi-agent credit assignment, non-stationarity from co-adapting agents, or continuous-action MARL — those are introduced only in Chapter 9 (outside this reader's range).
section: 8.1 Deep Value Function Approximation; 8.2.1 Advantages of Learning a Policy
conditions: n/a
limits: Bounded to the algorithms and experiments presented in Chapter 8 as extracted; does not assess Chapter 9's multi-agent extensions.

statement: The DQN component ablation (Figure 8.3) and the REINFORCE/A2C/PPO comparison (Figure 8.6) are each run on one fixed, small, single-agent grid-world task (8x8 level-based foraging with a single item) with a fixed roster of one agent; the book does not claim these results transfer to different task sizes, different numbers of items/agents, or different observation/action spaces — claims of generalization beyond the reported experiments would not be supported by them.
section: 8.1.4 Putting It All Together: Deep Q-Networks; 8.2.7 Policy Gradient Algorithms in Practice
conditions: n/a
limits: Applies specifically to the two named figures/experiments; does not evaluate any other reported experiment in the book.

statement: curator_connection: the deadly-triad mechanism the book describes for single-agent deep Q-learning (off-policy data + function approximation + bootstrapped targets → possible divergence, pp. 216-218) names the same three ingredients present in centralized value/critic updates that an HMASD-style algorithm relies on; this is a conceptual parallel only — the book's deadly-triad discussion is single-agent and offers no multi-agent evidence, so it cannot be cited as a finding about any HMASD direction's actual training stability, only as a candidate explanatory frame to check against HMASD's own diagnostics.
conditions: n/a
limits: Purely conceptual; no HMASD-specific evidence is asserted or implied by the source text.
